name: Strength
upright: Untrusted input tamed: validated on the server, encoded on output, bound into queries, with errors that reveal nothing.
reversed: Raw input let loose: string-built SQL, unchecked buffers, stack traces shown to strangers and code changes nobody logged.
vision: A calm figure in a white robe closes a lion's jaws with bare hands. The lion may roar only the words inked on the figure's own palm; the list on the lion's paw counts for nothing. A command the lion roars disguised as a name is pressed into a stone mold with fixed blanks, where it can only ever be a name. Thorns spat into the garland of flowers come out as harmless paintings of thorns. When a roar fails, the figure tells the crowd only that it failed, never why. Above their head the infinity sign has one loop marked check, one marked use, and a mouse slips through the crossing between them.
decode: Jaws held shut; only the words on the figure's palm count → allow-list input validation enforced on the server; client-side checks are trivially bypassed.
The stone mold with fixed blanks → parameterized queries (prepared statements): input stays data and is never executed as SQL.
Thorns turned into paintings of thorns → output encoding: special characters are escaped, so the browser shows a script instead of running it (XSS).
Only that it failed, never why → secure error handling: a generic message for users, the details kept in protected server logs.
A mouse slipping between check and use → race condition (TOCTOU): an attacker changes the resource after it is checked but before it is used.
facts: Buffer overflows come from missing bounds checks: input longer than the buffer overwrites adjacent memory, such as a return address. Check every input's length.
XSS abuses a user's trust in a website; CSRF abuses a website's trust in the user's browser. Output encoding stops XSS; anti-CSRF tokens stop CSRF.
Maintenance hooks are developer backdoors that bypass access controls; they must be removed before code reaches production.
trap: The collective once trusted the validation running in the browser. Attackers bypass the browser entirely, so validate on the server with an allow-list and bind input with parameterized queries.
